lines.text: Every day, a bank's fraud model raises thousands of alerts, and most of the high-scoring ones are false alarms.
Real fraud hides where no single alert can see it: on other cards, on shared devices, in cases the bank already closed.
This is FraudLens: a team of AI investigators that works every case on TigerGraph, and proves every claim it makes.
An alert comes in: a model score, a customer complaint, or an analyst's hunch. A lead investigator sends four specialists after it.
Every question goes to TigerGraph through the official MCP server, read-only, limited to eighteen installed queries.
A model trained on the bank's own closed cases estimates the odds. Code, not the language model, owns the policy, the numbers and the approvals.
Here's an analyst's lead: several cards this month made purchases from the same unusual phone.
The network specialist asks TigerGraph who else used this phone. Nineteen other cardholders in eight days, the phone new to every one of them, every session behind an anonymous proxy.
The precedent specialist searches case memory with a graph-filtered vector search, and finds four confirmed cases from the summer, with the very same device.
It fits none of the five known patterns. So the agent names a new one: a shared-device ring.
Every finding moves a calibrated ledger. At ninety-seven percent, on independent evidence, the policy says: stop investigating, and act.
Block the card, file a suspicious activity report, and watch all nineteen connected cards. Every action cites its rule, and who must approve it.
Nothing is taken on faith. Every claim carries the exact query behind it. Press re-prove, and it runs again, live, on TigerGraph Savanna.
The suspicious activity report is written to FinCEN's standard: who, what, when, where, how, and why.
Most alerts aren't fraud. This one scored ninety percent: a thousand dollars, from a device the card had never used.
Our transaction model puts it below one percent. So the agent verifies before it blocks, and plans for every reply.
On October's high-score alerts, which the model never saw, the bank's own score ranks a real fraud above a false alarm sixty times in a hundred. Ours does it ninety-three times.
The agent only executes automatic actions. A team lead can't approve a suspicious activity report; only a fraud manager can.
And every decision is written back to the graph, so the next investigation remembers it.
With no alert at all, the monitor sweeps the graph by itself, and finds rings that nobody reported.
FraudLens. Agentic, calibrated, and provable. The model predicts. TigerGraph proves.
